1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4.name: Alekhine's Defence
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4.strategy: The main line: the pawn supports e5, claims the centre and opens the c1-bishop. White takes a space advantage in the middle, which is just what Black's defence invites, since Black plans to undermine the advanced pawns later with piece play.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4.name: Alekhine's Defence: Two Pawns Attack
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4.strategy: Hits the knight a second time and claims still more space, for a broad pawn centre. The advanced pawns become targets for Black's pieces, so White has to bring the rest of the army into play quickly to show that the space is a strength, not an overextension.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4.strategy: Attacks the knight, which has no defender, but the retreat to b6 hits the bishop in return, so it has to move again. The bishop keeps its sights on f7, but White has spent time on a piece Black can harass.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Nc3.name: Alekhine's Defence: Sämisch Attack
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Nc3.background: Friedrich Sämisch chose it against Alexander Alekhine in 1921, when the defence first appeared.
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Nc3.strategy: Attacks the undefended knight and invites a trade on c3, after which White has doubled pawns in return for quick development or a bigger centre, depending on the recapture. A way to avoid the sharpest lines, at the price of the ambitious space grab.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.b3.name: Alekhine's Defence: Welling Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, which would defend e5 along the long diagonal without committing the d-pawn. It is slow: for now e5 stands unsupported, and Black can attack it before the bishop arrives.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Na3.name: Alekhine's Defence: Buckley Attack
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Na3.strategy: A knight on the rim: it may reach c4 later, but it does nothing for the centre, and the e5 pawn is left without support. Black can attack that pawn at once, and White has spent a tempo on a square the knight will want to leave.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 Nb6.strategy: Retreats with a tempo: the knight attacks the bishop, which must move again, and from b6 it eyes c4 and d5, the squares the bishop wanted. Black pays another knight move, the usual price of this defence, but gains the time back.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 c6.strategy: Defends the knight with a pawn instead of retreating it. If White trades bishop for knight and takes space with d4, Black gets a sound structure and a half-open c-file, but a cramped game against the e5 pawn and a c8-bishop that still has to find its way out.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 e6.strategy: Defends the knight with the e-pawn and opens the f8-bishop. If White trades on d5, the recapture leaves Black solid but passive: the c8-bishop is still shut in and the e5 pawn takes space. Black accepts a slower game rather than a lively knight.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 Nb6 4.Bb3.strategy: Keeps the bishop on the diagonal aimed at f7 and out of the knight's reach. But the bishop has few safe squares there: the knight covers a4, c4 and d5, Black's pawns cover e6, and its own pawns block a2 and c2, so a pawn attack on it needs care.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 Nb6 4.Bd3.strategy: Puts the bishop out of the knight's reach with an eye on the h7 pawn, but it gives up the pressure on f7 and blocks the d-pawn, so the centre cannot be built with d4. The e5 pawn has to be held by pieces or by f4.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 Nb6 4.Be2.strategy: Retreats to a safe, modest square and clears the way to castling, but the bishop has spent two moves to get back nearly where it started and no longer eyes f7. Black gets time to challenge the e5 pawn and the centre.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 Nb6 4.Bb3 c5.strategy: Threatens ...c4, which would trap the bishop: the knight covers a4 and c4, and the white pawns on a2 and c2 take away the other squares. It also stakes a claim on d4 and starts queenside play for Black.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 Nb6 4.Bb3 e6.strategy: Shuts the b3-bishop's diagonal for good and opens the f8-bishop. Black gets a solid structure and no worries about f7, but the c8-bishop is locked in behind its own pawns and the e5 pawn cramps the position for a long time.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 Nb6 4.Bb3 d5.strategy: Takes space and blocks the bishop's diagonal with a pawn. White can capture en passant, which brings a pawn to d6 and opens the diagonal against f7 again, so Black has to develop with care.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 Nb6 4.Bb3 c5 5.d.name: Alekhine's Defence: Kmoch Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 Nb6 4.Bb3 c5 5.d.strategy: The main answer: it guards c4, so ...c4 can be met by a pawn capture and the bishop stays on its diagonal. White settles for a modest set-up instead of an immediate fight for the centre, and the e5 pawn, no longer backed by a d-pawn, has to be held by pieces.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 Nb6 4.Bb3 c5 5.Q.strategy: Guards c4 with the queen, so that ...c4 simply loses a pawn: Bxc4 Nxc4 Qxc4. The queen comes out early, which costs time, but it also holds the e5 pawn.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.Bc4 Nb6 4.Bb3 c5 5.c.strategy: Gives the bishop the c2 square, so ...c4 can be met by Bc2. White keeps the bishop, but Black gains queenside space with a pawn on c4, and the c3 pawn takes a square from the knight and leaves d3 without a pawn guard.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6.strategy: The natural retreat: the knight keeps an eye on the c4 pawn and can return to d5 as soon as the c-pawn advances. Black accepts being driven back again, trusting that the advanced white pawns will become targets later.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nf4.name: Alekhine's Defence: The Squirrel
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nf4.strategy: Jumps to an unstable square without support. White can win time by attacking the knight, and it will have to move again to a worse square; Black has moved the same piece three times for nothing.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb4.strategy: Jumps away to b4, where the knight is just as offside as on b6 and can be harassed again. After d4, the natural ...d6 runs into Qa4+, which checks the king and attacks the knight at once; Black loses time and gets nothing for it.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5.name: Alekhine's Defence: Two Pawns Attack, Lasker Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5.strategy: Chases the knight a second time and grabs more space, but gives up control of d5, where the knight happily returns. The pawns on c5 and e5 stretch White's position, and they must prove strong rather than overextended.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.b3.name: Alekhine's Defence: Steiner Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.b3.strategy: Supports the c4 pawn, which frees the f1-bishop from guarding it, and prepares to put a bishop on the long diagonal, where it also backs up e5. A flexible but slow set-up that lets Black challenge the advanced pawns.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.a4.name: Alekhine's Defence: Two Pawns Attack, Tate Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.a4.background: The idea of this early rook lift probably came from the American International Master Emory Tate, for whom the line is named. Mariya Muzychuk, Lu Shanglei and Nazar Firman have tried it with some success.
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.a4.strategy: A tricky sideline: the a-pawn threatens to chase the knight again, with a pawn sacrifice on e6 in mind to disturb Black's development. Black can stop that, and White then swings a rook along the third rank towards the kingside. It needs accurate answers, but the plan is slow and leaves Black a strong centre.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.d4.strategy: The main move: the d-pawn backs up e5 and completes a broad pawn centre, so the space gained by the two advances is held rather than left hanging. Black has to challenge it with pieces and pawn breaks, and the game often reaches the main lines of the 3.d4 move order.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Nd5.strategy: The only square: the knight returns to d5, which White's last move left without a pawn to challenge it, so it now stands there as an outpost. White's pawns on c5 and e5 are far advanced and need support.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Nc4.strategy: Hangs the knight: the f1-bishop takes it at once, since nothing defends c4, and Black has nothing to show for it.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Na4.strategy: Hangs the knight: the queen takes it along the open d1-a4 diagonal, and nothing defends the square.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Nd5 5.Bc.strategy: Develops with tempo: the knight on d5 has no defender, so Black has to support it or move it. The bishop also eyes f7, and White keeps the choice of trading it for the knight or leaving it as a thorn.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Nd5 5.Nc.strategy: Attacks the undefended knight and invites a trade that helps White's development. Black can trade, or defend d5 with a pawn, and White hopes the space on c5 and e5 outweighs the time spent.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Nd5 5.d4.strategy: Supports the c5 and e5 pawns with a pawn at once, so Black cannot simply attack them, and builds a broad centre. The price is time: the knight on d5 is left alone, and Black can undermine the chain from the side.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Nd5 5.Bc.strategy: Defends the knight with a pawn and opens the f8-bishop. Black accepts a solid pawn chain on the light squares, at the price of shutting in the c8-bishop for now, and keeps the strong knight on d5.

Defends the knight with the c-pawn and opens the queen's diagonal towards b6 and a5, from where it presses on the c5 pawn. Black takes c6 from the b8-knight, but keeps the knight on its outpost and the e-pawn flexible.
Walks to b4 instead of defending the knight, which gives up the outpost on d5. White gains time chasing it, and meanwhile nothing pressures the advanced pawns.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Nd5 5.Bc.name: Alekhine's Defence: Hunt Variation, Lasker Simul Gambit
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Nd5 5.Bc.strategy: Brings a second attacker to d5 and develops, but leaves c5 and e5 without pawn support, so ...d6 hits both at once. White plays for quick piece play and has to be ready to give up a pawn for it.

Supports the c5 and e5 pawns with a pawn, so Black's strike at the chain loses its sting, and keeps the bishop's pressure on d5. White holds the space it has grabbed, and Black has to undermine the chain from the flank in a strategic fight.

Trades the bishop for the knight and removes the outpost, but Black recaptures with the e-pawn, which blocks the centre and leaves a solid pawn on d5. White keeps the space, but loses its most active piece.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Nd5 5.Bc.name: Alekhine's Defence: Two Pawns Attack, Mikenas Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Nd5 5.Bc.strategy: Attacks both advanced pawns at once, the point of the whole line: neither is supported, so something has to give. It also opens the c8-bishop, and White's space grab on the queenside starts to cost something.

Trades off the second attacker of d5, which takes the pressure off the knight's square. White recaptures with a pawn and gets open lines for the pieces, and the unsupported c5 and e5 pawns can still be attacked afterwards, but with less point than at once.

Defends the knight a second time with a pawn, so White's knight cannot win it by trading. Black stays solid, but spends a tempo on a pawn move while the advanced white pawns stand, and White can use the time to support them.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.c5 Nd5 5.Nc.strategy: Removes the attacker rather than defending the knight, and forces White to recapture with a pawn. White gets open lines for the pieces and doubled c-pawns; Black gets a healthy structure and a free hand against the advanced pawns.

Defends the knight with the e-pawn and opens the f8-bishop. If White trades knights on d5, the recapture leaves a solid pawn there that blocks the centre, and White has to hold the c5 and e5 pawns against Black's play from the flank.

Defends the knight with the c-pawn and opens the queen's diagonal towards b6 and a5, so the c5 pawn can be pressed. The pawn move costs a tempo and takes c6 from the b8-knight, but the knight keeps its outpost.

Recaptures towards the centre, which opens the d-file and the c1-bishop for quick development. The c5 and e5 pawns lose their natural support and can be attacked, but White can meet the attack by taking on d6 and trading the loose pawns off for an even game.

Recaptures with the b-pawn, which keeps the d-pawn at home to support the advanced pawns with a central advance. The price is doubled c-pawns and an isolated a-pawn, so White plays for the centre at the cost of the queenside structure.
Moves the queen out of attack with a threat to the c3 knight, but does not recapture: the knight simply steps away to e4, where nothing attacks it, and White has lost a piece for nothing.
Attacks c5 and e5 at once, neither of which has any pawn behind it, and opens the c8-bishop. White cannot easily support both, so the space gained by the pawn advances now comes under pressure.
Attacks the base of the c5 pawn from the side, and it has no pawn behind it. White has to resolve the tension at once, and Black gets an open file against the queenside while the e5 pawn stays loose.
Develops with a direct threat to e5, but it attacks only one of the two loose pawns, and White can defend it while developing. The pawn strike that hits both at once is more precise.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6.name: Alekhine's Defence
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6.strategy: Hits the head of the pawn chain at once, the standard way to challenge the space White has taken, and opens the c8-bishop. White now has to decide how to meet ...dxe5, and that choice sets the character of the game.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 b5.name: Alekhine's Defence: O'Sullivan Gambit
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 b5.strategy: A pawn sacrifice that tries to lure the bishop to b5, a vulnerable square. White can simply take the pawn, so Black needs more than hope for compensation.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 c5.strategy: Strikes at the base of White's chain at once, but White simply takes: dxc5 removes the b6 retreat and opens the d-file against the undefended knight on d5. Black is a pawn down and has to untangle the knight immediately.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3.name: Alekhine's Defence: Modern Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3.background: The most common variation of Alekhine's Defence.
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and prepares to retake on e5 with the knight if Black takes. White accepts a modest space advantage and relies on piece play rather than a full pawn centre; Black's natural test is to pin the knight.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4.name: Alekhine's Defence
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4.strategy: Drives the knight away again and takes more space,. White commits the c-pawn to the centre and has to decide between a safe trade and a maximalist centre, while the knight can only go to b6.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Bc4.name: Alekhine's Defence: Balogh Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Bc4.background: The first recorded game with it is Canal-Colle, Karlovy Vary 1929, which White resigned after Black's 40th move. Unlike several other sidelines, it is fairly popular.
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Bc4.strategy: Attacks the undefended knight and commits White to recapturing on e5 with the d-pawn. The retreat to b6 hits the bishop in return, and the attacking chances come at the cost of a thinner centre; there are traps for the unwary.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6.strategy: The only safe square: the knight retreats and keeps an eye on the c4 pawn, and Black threatens to take on e5 and trade queens, which would cost White the right to castle. White must settle the tension in the centre at once.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb4.strategy: Walks into Qa4+, which checks the king and attacks the knight at once. Black cannot save both and loses a piece.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nf6.strategy: Goes back to f6, where the e5 pawn takes it: Black loses the knight for a pawn at best.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.exd.name: Alekhine's Defence: Exchange Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.exd.strategy: Takes first, which removes the threat of ...dxe5 and a queen trade that would cost White castling. White settles for a modest space advantage and a more strategic game, and Black's way of recapturing decides how sharp it gets.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4.name: Alekhine's Defence: Four Pawns Attack
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4.background: Not particularly popular in practice, because many White players are wary of entering so sharp a line that Black may have prepared.
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4.strategy: Prepares to retake on e5 with the f-pawn and so keep a huge pawn centre. The most ambitious try, but the pawns must be used: Black will undermine them, and the game is sharp and tactical.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops and prepares to retake on e5 with the knight, while keeping the d4 pawn in the centre. But it walks into ...Bg4, which pins the knight to the queen, and White has not yet settled the pawn tension.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.c5.name: Alekhine's Defence: Hunt Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.c5.strategy: Chases the knight a third time, but gives up control of d5 and leaves two advanced pawns facing the d6 pawn. Black can take on c5 and trade queens, which leaves the white king uncastled and the knight settled on d5.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.exd.strategy: The sharper recapture: Black keeps a pawn majority in the centre and aims pieces at White's c4 and d4 pawns. The usual plan is a fianchetto of the king's bishop, with a knight on b6 and c6 bearing down on the pawns.

The solid recapture: a compact pawn structure and an open e-file, but fewer chances to fight the white pawns. The game turns positional and rests on piece play, with ...d5 as the way to free the position later.

Recaptures with the queen and keeps the pawn structure intact. The queen is exposed to c5, which attacks it and the knight together; ...Qe6+ gets out of the fork with check, but Black will sooner or later have to deal with that threat.
Develops while keeping the king's knight off f3, where ...Bg4 would make it a target. White delays kingside development so that Black has less to harass, and the knight on c3 adds pressure on d5.
Develops the king's knight and defends d4, the natural way to hold the centre. But on f3 the knight becomes a target for ...Bg4, which lets Black trade it off and loosen White's hold on d4.

Develops the bishop to the square that defends d4 and keeps the king's knight at home, so ...Bg4 has no knight to hit. White still has to find a way to bring out the remaining pieces without loosening the centre.

Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop: from g7 it presses along the long diagonal on d4, and Black attacks White's pawn centre with pieces instead of defending against it. The central pawn majority gives that plan its support.
Attacks the d4 pawn at once, but d5 drives the knight away with a gain of space, and it has to settle on a square like e5 or b4. Black loses time unless the knight finds a use there.
Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain at once. But it can be harassed: White can offer a trade with Bd3 or chase it with g4, and the bishop then has to give up the diagonal.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4.strategy: The main reply: Black strikes at the head of the chain at once. After the recapture with the f-pawn the f-file is half-open for White and Black can aim pieces at d4 and e5, the weak points of the big centre.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4.name: Alekhine's Defence: Four Pawns Attack, Fianchetto Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4.strategy: A fianchetto: the bishop on g7 will press along the long diagonal against d4 and e5, tackling the big centre from a distance. A quieter reply, but it gives White other attacking plans on the kingside.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4.name: Alekhine's Defence: Four Pawns Attack, Trifunovic Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4.strategy: A quieter way to meet the big centre: the bishop develops outside the pawn chain before ...e6 would shut it in, and the capture on e5 waits. Black delays the central fight instead of starting it at once.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4.name: Alekhine's Defence: Four Pawns Attack, Cambridge Gambit
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4.background: Named the Planinc Variation after Albin Planinc, who championed it in the 1970s. The correspondence player Michael Schirmer took it up in the 1990s, and British grandmaster Nigel Davies noted his games in a book on the defence.
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4.strategy: A gambit: if White takes the pawn, the centre falls apart after ...dxe5 and a queen trade, and Black wins the pawn back with a better structure. It is objectively unsound, since declining it gives White an edge with the centre intact.

The natural recapture: it keeps three pawns in the centre and half-opens the f-file for White's pieces. But the f-pawn no longer stands behind e5, and Black can attack the pawns on e5 and d4 with pieces.

Recaptures with the d-pawn and allows the queens off: ...Qxd1+ forces Kxd1, so White loses the right to castle, and Black develops with ...Bg4+. The advanced pawns on c4, e5 and f4 lose the centre pawn that backed them.
Develops, but leaves the pawn on e5 free to take: it attacks both d4 and f4, and after ...exd4 even a recapture leaves White a pawn down. White has given up the strong centre for nothing.

Attacks d4, the base of White's pawn chain, at once. The whole defence aims at knocking out the support of the centre, and the knight adds a second attacker to the pawn while White is still developing.

Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 closes it in, and keeps ...c5 available before the knight commits. It does not hit d4 at once, but the game usually reaches the same positions as the knight move, with White's big centre under pressure.

Strikes at the base of White's centre with a pawn instead of a piece. It is riskier than the knight move: d5 gains space and takes c6 and e6 away from Black's pieces, so Black has to play accurately not to be squeezed.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.Nf3.strategy: Pins the knight to the queen and loosens White's hold on the centre. The knight cannot leave f3 without losing the queen, which means the e5 pawn depends on the d-pawn alone.

Clears the e5 pawn at once, but the knight recaptures on a strong central post that Black cannot easily challenge, and White's pawns on d4 and c4 keep their grip on the centre. Black passes up the ...Bg4 pin and has to find play elsewhere.

Heads for the king's bishop on the long diagonal, which fights White's centre from a distance. If White trades on d6, Black recaptures into a solid, compact game; if not, the tension on e5 stays. The price is that the ...Bg4 pin waits.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.Nf3.name: Alekhine's Defence: Modern Variation, Alekhine Gambit
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.Nf3.strategy: Unpins by interposing the bishop, but it gives Black ...dxe5: after Nxe5 Bxe2 White must recapture with the queen and lose d4 to ...Qxd4, or with the king and give up castling.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.Nf3.name: Alekhine's Defence: Modern Variation, Vitolins Attack
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.Nf3.strategy: Gains space, but takes away the d-pawn's support of e5 while the knight is still pinned. Black can simply take ...dxe5, and the knight cannot recapture without losing the queen to ...Bxd1.

Settles the tension before Black can use the pin: the e5 pawn trades itself off, so there is no ...dxe5 to pry at d4. White keeps its d4 and c4 pawns and a modest space edge, and Black gets a freer, more open game.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4.name: Alekhine's Defence: Modern Variation, Main Line
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: The main line: the bishop develops outside the pawn chain and pins the knight to the queen, so the knight cannot simply recapture on e5. Black keeps the tension in the centre and stands ready to trade bishop for knight, which undermines White's centre pawns.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 g6.name: Alekhine's Defence: Modern Variation, Alburt Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 g6.background: Played in the thirteenth game of the Match of the Century between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer. Lev Alburt has also played it frequently.
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 g6.strategy: Leaves White's pawn chain alone for now and prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, so that it fights the e5 pawn from a distance. Black accepts less space for a flexible, solid set-up and plans to undermine the centre later.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 dxe5.name: Alekhine's Defence: Modern Variation, Larsen Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 dxe5.background: Named after Bent Larsen, who employed the line in the 1965 Candidates.
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 dxe5.strategy: Settles the tension at once and frees both the c8-bishop and the d-file. The price is that the white knight lands on e5, where it is strong and hard to dislodge, so White keeps a small edge in space and Black has to find active development.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Nc6.name: Alekhine's Defence: Modern Variation, Larsen-Haakert Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the other knight and adds pressure on d4 and e5 at once. It takes the c6 square from the pawn that could have supported the knight on d5, and White can gain space with tempo by hitting that knight with the c-pawn.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Nb6.name: Alekhine's Defence: Modern Variation, Schmid Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Nb6.strategy: Retreats the knight before White has driven it away. That saves White the time the c-pawn would have cost, so White can develop on its own terms, while Black keeps a flexible structure but has given up the knight's central post.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.Be.strategy: The main line: the bishop breaks the pin and prepares castling, so the knight is free again to recapture on e5. White keeps a broad pawn centre and a small edge in space, and leaves Black to decide whether to trade bishop for knight.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.c4.name: Alekhine's Defence: Modern Variation, Alekhine Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.c4.strategy: Hits the knight with a pawn at once, so it has to move again, and White gains space. The cost is time and a looser grip on d4, but the e5 chain stays intact and White builds a broad pawn centre that Black must learn to undermine.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.h3.name: Alekhine's Defence: Modern Variation, Panov Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.h3.strategy: Asks the bishop what it wants, but Black is happy to give it up for the knight: White recaptures with the queen, gets the bishop pair, and finds the centre pawns easier to attack than before.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.Be.name: Alekhine's Defence: Modern Variation, Flohr Variation
1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.Be.strategy: Supports the knight on d5 with a pawn and covers b5, so the knight keeps its post in the centre. A solid, compact choice, at the price of the c6 square, which the b8-knight loses.

Backs up the knight on d5 with a pawn and opens the king's bishop, leaving the tension on e5 as it is. Black accepts a compact, slightly cramped set-up and waits for the moment to strike at White's centre with a pawn break.
Takes the pawn at once, but after Nxe5 Bxe2 Qxe2 White has a knight on e5 that is hard to dislodge and a lead in development, and Black has trouble making progress. Black has to defend patiently.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.c4.strategy: The only sensible retreat: Nb4 runs into Qa4+ and loses the knight. From b6 the knight eyes the c4 pawn, and the pin on f3 stays, so Black keeps the pressure on White's big centre, which White now has to resolve.
Runs into Qa4+, which attacks the knight on b4 at once and leaves Black a piece down for little.

Trades the pinning bishop for the knight at the wrong moment: the queen recaptures and, with the c-pawn, attacks the knight on d5 a second time, so Black must retreat it and has lost a tempo as well as the bishop pair.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 g6 5.Bc4.strategy: The main move: the bishop develops with tempo against the knight on d5 and keeps the c-pawn free. Once the knight leaves, the bishop eyes f7, and White gains time and lasting kingside pressure while Black has to find a way to undermine the d4 and e5 pawns.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 g6 5.c4.strategy: Challenges the knight with a pawn and commits to a broad pawn centre. Once the knight has retreated, White can settle the tension by trading on d6 and keep a modest space edge in a calmer game than the main line.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 g6 5.Be2.strategy: A quiet development that prepares castling and guards the knight on f3 without committing a pawn. It lets the knight keep its post on d5, so Black completes the fianchetto and attacks d4 and e5 without any pressure from White's pieces.

1.e4 Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 g6 5.Bc4.strategy: The natural retreat, which hits the bishop and makes it decide. Black has spent three moves on this knight in return for a compact, solid set-up with the king's bishop to follow, accepting that White's bishop keeps a good diagonal.

Guards the knight with a pawn instead of retreating it, so a trade on d5 only gives Black a central pawn. It is solid but slow: c6 is taken from the b8-knight, the fianchetto is still to come, and White keeps the initiative.

Props up the knight with the e-pawn, so Bxd5 exd5 leaves Black a sound pawn on d5. But the pawn shuts in the c8-bishop and lets White trade off the centre and open the e-file, so Black spends the next moves catching up.

Keeps the bishop instead of allowing a trade on c4. From b3 it stays on the diagonal to f7, so Black has to watch that square throughout, while White keeps its space and the initiative on the kingside.

Retreats to a safe square where the bishop cannot be harassed, and prepares castling at once. It gives up the diagonal to f7, though, so Black can complete the fianchetto and challenge d4 and e5 without anxiety.

Keeps the bishop on a diagonal towards the kingside, but it stands in front of the queen, so d4 loses its defender: after ...dxe5, Nxe5 drops the d4 pawn to ...Qxd4, so White has to recapture with the d-pawn. A playable, passive retreat.

Completes the fianchetto: the bishop attacks e5 along the long diagonal, challenging White's whole pawn centre, and Black is ready to castle. The cost is that White's pieces aim at f7 and the kingside, so Black has to hold that side together.
Threatens ...a4, which would push the bishop back to a2 and gain space on the queenside. The price is time: a pawn move on the wing while White leads in development and keeps the initiative.
Shuts the b3-bishop's diagonal with a pawn, so f7 is no longer a target. The cost is a passive set-up: the c8-bishop is hemmed in, and White keeps its space and the freer game.
